summary: Oral ribavirin is a synthetic guanosine nucleoside antiviral used in combination with (peg)interferon alfa (and historically as part of multi-drug regimens) for chronic hepatitis C; it is NOT effective as monotherapy for HCV. Dosing is weight-based, generally about 800-1400 mg/day in two divided doses taken with food. It carries a BOXED WARNING for dose-related hemolytic anemia (which can worsen cardiac disease and has caused fatal/non-fatal MI) and for significant teratogenic and embryocidal effects: it is contraindicated in pregnant women and in the male partners of pregnant women. Because of a long multi-dose half-life (~12 days) and persistence in tissues, effective contraception is required during treatment and for 9 months after in women (and female partners of treated men) and 6 months after in treated men.
indications: Chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection in combination with peginterferon alfa / interferon alfa (and as part of approved combination regimens)
Used in patients with compensated liver disease; not for hepatitis C monotherapy

dosage.c: Chronic HCV with PegIntron (peginterferon alfa-2b) - by weight
dosage.d: <66 kg: 800 mg/day; 66-80 kg: 1000 mg/day; 81-105 kg: 1200 mg/day; >105 kg: 1400 mg/day - all in 2 divided doses
dosage.n: Take morning and evening with food

dosage.c: Chronic HCV with peginterferon alfa-2a (e.g. genotype 1/4)
dosage.d: <75 kg: 1000 mg/day; >=75 kg: 1200 mg/day in 2 divided doses

dosage.c: Dose modification for anemia (no cardiac disease)
dosage.d: Reduce to 600 mg/day if hemoglobin <10 g/dL; discontinue if Hb <8.5 g/dL
Reduce dose if Hb falls >=2 g/dL during any 4-week period; permanently discontinue if Hb <12 g/dL after 4 weeks of reduced dose
~15 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses (capsules/oral solution by weight bands)

admin: Take with food, at the same times each day (morning and evening)
Swallow capsules whole - do not open, crush, or break them (tablets per their own instructions)
Always use in combination with peginterferon/interferon (or approved combination) - never as monotherapy
Confirm a negative pregnancy test before starting and ensure two reliable contraception methods
Obtain baseline CBC, then check hemoglobin at weeks 2 and 4 and periodically thereafter
Assess for and optimise cardiac status before treatment in patients with heart disease
moa: Ribavirin is a synthetic nucleoside (guanosine) analogue with broad in-vitro activity against RNA and DNA viruses. Several mechanisms are proposed for its anti-HCV effect, including inhibition of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (depleting intracellular GTP pools), interference with viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and 5'-cap formation, immunomodulation favouring a Th1 antiviral response, and induction of lethal mutagenesis ('error catastrophe') in the viral genome. Its clinical antiviral benefit in HCV is realised only in combination with interferon-based therapy; ribavirin alone does not durably suppress HCV.

absolute: Men whose female partners are pregnant
Known hypersensitivity (including severe reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, TEN, erythema multiforme) to ribavirin
Co-administration with didanosine (risk of fatal hepatic failure, neuropathy, pancreatitis, lactic acidosis)
Decompensated hepatic disease (Child-Pugh B/C) when combined with interferon (per interferon labeling)
relative: Pre-existing cardiac disease (anemia may precipitate MI - assess before and monitor during)
Significant or unstable cardiac disease (do not use)
Renal impairment (CrCl <50 mL/min) - not recommended for some formulations
Pre-existing anemia or low baseline hemoglobin
monitor: ECG in patients with pre-existing cardiac disease
Hepatic function and signs of decompensation

preg: BOXED WARNING / CONTRAINDICATED. Significant teratogenic and embryocidal effects occur in all animal species exposed to ribavirin. Ribavirin is contraindicated in pregnant women and in the male partners of pregnant women. Avoid pregnancy: women of childbearing potential and female partners of male patients must use effective contraception during therapy and for 9 months (women) and 6 months (treated men) after the last dose. Because of a multiple-dose half-life of ~12 days and tissue persistence up to ~6 months, two negative pregnancy tests before starting and monthly testing during and after treatment are required, and a ribavirin pregnancy registry exists for exposed pregnancies.
lact: It is not known whether ribavirin is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in breastfed infants, a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or the drug, taking into account the importance of the drug to the mother.
renal: Ribavirin and its metabolites accumulate in renal impairment, increasing the risk of severe hemolytic anemia. For some capsule/tablet formulations, use is not recommended when creatinine clearance is below 50 mL/min. If used in renal impairment, reduce the dose, monitor hemoglobin very closely, and do not give to patients on hemodialysis with standard regimens unless benefit clearly outweighs risk.
hepatic: Ribavirin combination therapy is contraindicated in patients with decompensated liver disease (Child-Pugh class B or C) because of the risk of hepatic decompensation with the interferon component. Use only in compensated liver disease and monitor hepatic function.

major: Didanosine (ddI) - contraindicated; fatal/nonfatal hepatic failure, peripheral neuropathy, pancreatitis, symptomatic lactic acidosis
Zidovudine and stavudine (worsened anemia / mitochondrial toxicity - avoid or monitor closely)
Azathioprine (ribavirin inhibits IMPDH - risk of severe myelotoxicity/pancytopenia)
moderate: Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors generally (mitochondrial toxicity)
Drugs that worsen cardiac or pulmonary status (in the context of anemia)
minor: Antacids (may reduce ribavirin bioavailability if taken together)
interactions.food: Take with food - food increases ribavirin absorption/exposure
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - alcohol accelerates progression of hepatitis C liver disease
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor hemoglobin/CBC, pregnancy tests, TSH, LFTs; hemolysis raises indirect bilirubin and uric acid

serious: Severe hemolytic anemia (may precipitate fatal/non-fatal myocardial infarction)
Pulmonary symptoms - dyspnoea, pulmonary infiltrates, pneumonitis
rare: Severe cutaneous reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, erythema multiforme)
Aplastic anemia / pure red cell aplasia

monitoring: Hemoglobin/CBC at baseline, weeks 2 and 4, then periodically (hemolytic anemia)
Monthly pregnancy tests during and for the post-treatment contraception period
ECG before starting in patients with pre-existing cardiac disease
Hepatic function and signs of decompensation
Renal function (drug accumulates in renal impairment)
counsel: This medicine can cause severe birth defects - it must not be used in pregnancy, or by men whose partner is pregnant
Use two reliable contraception methods during treatment and for 6-9 months afterward as directed
Do not donate blood while taking it and for 6 months after
Take with food and swallow capsules whole; never take it alone - it is used with interferon
Report severe tiredness, breathlessness, chest pain, or palpitations (signs of anemia/heart strain)
Report low mood, thoughts of self-harm, severe rash, or breathing problems promptly
Avoid alcohol; keep all blood-test appointments
pk: Antiviral effect assessed over weeks of combination therapy; absorbed with Tmax ~1.5-3 h
Plasma peak ~1.5 to 3 hours after an oral dose (with food)
Multiple-dose half-life approximately 12 days; persists in non-plasma compartments up to ~6 months
Steady state reached after ~4 weeks of twice-daily dosing
Store capsules/tablets at 25 degrees C (excursions 15-30 degrees C); keep dry
pearls: BOXED WARNING (triple): hemolytic anemia (may cause fatal/non-fatal MI), teratogenicity/embryocidal effects, and monotherapy is NOT effective for hepatitis C.

Contraindicated in pregnancy AND in the male partners of pregnant women; contraception required during and for 9 months (women) / 6 months (men) after, due to ~12-day half-life and tissue persistence.
Always combine with (peg)interferon (or approved regimen) - never give alone for HCV.
Dose-related hemolytic anemia is the key toxicity: check Hb at weeks 2 and 4; assess cardiac disease before treatment.
Drug interaction landmines: didanosine (contraindicated), zidovudine/stavudine (anemia/mitochondrial toxicity), azathioprine (severe myelotoxicity).
This record covers ORAL ribavirin (HCV); inhaled ribavirin (Virazole) for RSV is a separate product with different dosing/cautions (also teratogenic - avoid healthcare-worker pregnancy exposure).
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember on the same day, with food. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose - do not double up. Try to keep the morning and evening doses about 12 hours apart. Tell your prescriber if you miss several doses.
overdose: No specific antidote. Acute overdose may worsen the known toxicities, principally hemolytic anemia and the adverse effects of the co-administered interferon (hepatic, cardiac, neuropsychiatric). Hemodialysis does not effectively remove ribavirin. Manage supportively with monitoring of hemoglobin and cardiac status, transfusion if needed, and symptomatic treatment.
